title: In Stunning Political Upset, Democrat Annie Andrews Flips South Carolina Senate Seat
snippet: Pediatrician Annie Andrews has secured a historic victory in South Carolina, ending a 28-year Democratic Senate drought in a state Donald Trump carried comfortably just two years ago.
content:
WASHINGTON — In a historic political shockwave, Democrat Annie Andrews has captured a U.S. Senate seat in deeply conservative South Carolina, ousting Republican candidate Darline Graham in a state President Donald Trump carried by 18 percentage points just two years ago.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Palmetto State in nearly three decades. The outcome represents a crucial pickup for Democrats, who entered election night aiming to erase a 53-47 Republican Senate majority.

A Divided GOP and a Controversial Candidacy

The Senate seat opened unexpectedly following the sudden death of long-serving Republican Senator Lindsey Graham in July. Following personal lobbying from President Trump, South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister, Darline Graham—a state employee with no previous political experience—to fill the vacancy and launch a campaign for a full term.

Although Graham secured the Republican nomination after defeating U.S. Representative Ralph Norman in an August runoff, internal party strife lingered. Norman publicly acknowledged that while he planned to vote for Graham, his family would not, and he declined to join her on the stump. Graham’s campaign was further plagued by missteps, including an August debate performance in which she admitted she was not "that informed on national security" and that the subject was "not my thing."

Recognizing the candidate's vulnerabilities, outside GOP organizations poured $27 million into the state to shore up her candidacy, while Democratic groups invested $24 million to pull off the flip. In an unusual display of bipartisanship, former South Carolina Republican Governor David Beasley teamed up with former Democratic Governor Jim Hodges to jointly endorse Andrews.

Broader National Headwinds

The high-stakes race reached a boiling point last week during a heated exchange where Graham lashed out at her opponent, calling Andrews "batshit crazy." Andrews turned the line back on her rival, asking South Carolinians whether wanting reduced prices on grocery bills and gasoline was truly crazy.

Political analysts attribute Andrews' victory to growing voter frustration over the administration's foreign policy and rising living costs, including sharp spikes in diesel fuel prices. South Carolina's shift served as a bellwether for wider Democratic gains across the country on Tuesday, as the party also picked up Senate seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Kansas, and Texas.
